title: Repository & Data Boundary
scopeHtml: Scope: what a repository is for, the data-source split, single source of truth, and the model boundary where DTOs and entities stop. Room, Retrofit and WorkManager API detail is A5.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does the repository pattern solve in an Android app, and what is the official guidance on what a repository is responsible for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates recite "abstraction over data sources". The signal is whether you know the concrete responsibilities and why callers must not touch data sources directly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A repository is the single entry point to one type of application data. It hides where data comes from (network, DB, file, memory), resolves conflicts between sources, centralizes writes, and holds data-level business rules. The ViewModel or use case asks the repository for "articles" and never knows if that came from Retrofit or Room. That is what lets me change a source, add caching, or fake it in tests without touching the UI layer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The Android data-layer guide lists five jobs: expose data to the rest of the app, centralize changes to the data, resolve conflicts between multiple sources, abstract sources from the rest of the app, and contain business logic. Naming convention: <Data>Repository, one per type of data (NewsRepository, PaymentsRepository), not one per screen.

 UI layer (Composable -> ViewModel)
        |
 [domain layer: optional use cases]
        |
 Data layer:  NewsRepository   <- only entry point
                 |        |
     NewsRemoteDataSource  NewsLocalDataSource
        (Retrofit)             (Room DAO)

Rules that follow: nothing above the repository holds a data source; data exposed is immutable (safe across threads, cannot be corrupted by callers); the repository exposes suspend functions for one-shot operations and Flow for data that changes over time.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface NewsRepository {
    fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>>      // changes over time -> Flow
    suspend fun refresh()                           // one-shot -> suspend
    suspend fun bookmark(id: String, value: Boolean)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Repository named after a screen (HomeScreenRepository): it then duplicates data other screens need.
  • ViewModel injecting both a DAO and an API "because it is simpler": the conflict-resolution logic ends up in the UI layer.
  • Returning mutable lists or entities that callers modify.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does every app need repositories? -> The guide's own simplest example has a repository that just proxies one source; it earns its place the moment a second source, cache, or business rule appears (see Q118).
  2. Can a repository depend on another repository? -> Yes, for aggregation (e.g. UserRepository over login and registration repos); keep the graph acyclic (see Q132).
  3. Where does business logic go: repository or use case? -> Data-shaped rules (merge, dedupe, conflict resolution) in the repository; cross-repository, screen-agnostic orchestration in a use case.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "abstracts the data source so we can swap Retrofit." Senior: lists the five responsibilities, explains one-repo-per-data-type, immutability for thread safety, and names the failure modes (pass-through, DTO leaks, god repository).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team let ViewModels call ApiService directly in 6 screens; when a cache was added, only 3 screens got it and users saw inconsistent data between tabs.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a repository and a data source, and when is it acceptable to merge them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the two-level structure and don't create ceremony or, worse, skip the split when it matters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A data source talks to exactly one backing store: a network API, a Room DAO, DataStore, a file. A repository composes zero to many data sources and owns the policy: which source to read, when to refresh, how to merge. With a single source and no policy, merging them is fine, but I split them the moment a second source arrives.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Data source = mechanism, repository = policy. The official guide names data sources <Data><Remote|Local>DataSource and warns against naming by implementation detail (UserSharedPreferencesDataSource) because callers should not know how data is stored. Exception: during a migration you may have two implementations behind one interface, and naming by technology is fine until the old one is deleted.

Repository decides:  read local first? refresh if older than 5 min? merge remote+local?
DataSource does:     execute call, switch to correct thread, return raw model

The guide also notes that a DAO is already an interface, so injecting it directly into a repository (no wrapper data source) is fine if there is no extra logic. Data sources should be main-safe on their own (Room, Retrofit and Ktor suspend APIs already are).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class NewsRemoteDataSource(
    private val api: NewsApi,
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
) {
    suspend fun latest(): List<NetworkArticle> = withContext(io) { api.latest() }
}

class NewsRepositoryImpl(
    private val remote: NewsRemoteDataSource,
    private val dao: ArticleDao,       // DAO injected directly: it is already a seam
) : NewsRepository { /* policy lives here */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping a DAO in a data source that forwards every method 1:1 (ceremony, zero seam gained).
  • Putting caching policy inside the data source, so two repositories using it disagree.
  • Data source exposing entities/DTOs and the repository passing them straight up.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where should the dispatcher switch happen? -> In the data source/repository, never in the caller (see Q114).
  2. How do you migrate SharedPreferences to DataStore safely? -> Interface the data source, two implementations, migrate behind the repository (see Q134).
  3. Is a "cache" a data source? -> It can be: an in-memory data source with a single responsibility, or private state in the repository when it is a pure optimization.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "remote and local data sources and a repository". Senior: mechanism vs policy, when to merge, why naming by technology leaks, DAO-as-seam.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A repo with API+DAO logic mixed in one 900-line class made a second source (a CMS file) impossible to add without breaking tests.

questions.promptHtml: When should a repository function be suspend, and when should it return Flow? Why not just return Flow everywhere?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common source of subtle bugs (one-shot data wrapped in flows, reads wrapped in suspend that never update).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One-shot operations such as a write, a login, or "refresh now" are suspend. Data that can change while someone is looking at it is a Flow. A write is a single event with a single outcome; a read is a stream of snapshots. Returning Flow for a one-shot call hides errors and makes callers first() it; returning suspend for observable data means the screen goes stale.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Official guidance: suspend for one-shot CRUD, Flow for notifications of change over time. In an offline-first repository, reads come from the local source as a Flow (Room re-emits when the table changes), and writes are suspend (they can fail crossing the network boundary, and an exception is the natural way to report that).

Read  : repo.observeX(): Flow<X>      cold, re-emits on DB invalidation
Write : repo.updateX(x)  suspend      completes or throws
Pull  : repo.refresh()   suspend      writes to DB; the read Flow reacts

Key trick: refresh() returns Unit, not data. Data arrives through the observed Flow. That keeps one path for data to reach the UI.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ArticlesVm(private val repo: NewsRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val articles = repo.observeArticles()
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

    fun onPullToRefresh() = viewModelScope.launch { repo.refresh() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• fun getUser(): Flow<User> backed by one network call: a one-element flow that nobody collects twice correctly.
  • suspend fun getCart(): Cart consumed by 3 screens: each caches its own copy, they drift.
  • Returning StateFlow from the repository: forces a hot, always-live holder and an initial value you may not have.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a Room Flow hot or cold? -> Cold per collector; each collection runs the query and re-runs on invalidation of the queried tables.
  2. What if the screen needs "latest value now" once? -> observeX().first() or a separate suspend read; do not duplicate state.
  3. How do errors travel in each? -> Suspend throws or returns Result; Flow completes exceptionally and catch ends the stream (see Q122).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Flow for live data, suspend otherwise." Senior: refresh returns Unit and data flows through one stream; why reads/writes differ in failure semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app returned suspend getProfile() on 4 screens; after editing the profile, 2 screens showed the old name until restart.

questions.promptHtml: Who is responsible for switching threads in the data layer: the ViewModel, the repository, or the data source? What does "main-safe" mean?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the contract: callers should not need to know which dispatcher to use.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The class that does the blocking work owns the thread switch. Data sources and repositories must be main-safe: safe to call from the main thread because they move expensive work off it themselves. The ViewModel just calls and never writes withContext(Dispatchers.IO). Dispatchers are injected so tests can control them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Retrofit suspend functions, Room suspend DAOs and Ktor are already main-safe (they use their own executors), so wrapping them in withContext(IO) is noise. You need a switch for blocking APIs: File reads, JSON parsing of a large body you do manually, sorting/filtering 10k items (use Dispatchers.Default for CPU work, IO for blocking IO). Rule of thumb: main-safety is a property of the function's contract, documented by the fact that callers never switch.

ViewModel (Main) --call--> Repository.suspend fun --(withContext if blocking)--> work

Hardcoding Dispatchers.IO makes tests non-deterministic (real threads, no virtual time); inject a CoroutineDispatcher (or a qualifier like @IoDispatcher in Hilt). Dispatcher mechanics belong to A1.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ReceiptStore(
    private val dir: File,
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,       // injected, tests pass StandardTestDispatcher
) {
    suspend fun read(id: String): String = withContext(io) { File(dir, id).readText() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Callers wrapping every repository call in withContext(IO) "to be safe".
  • Dispatchers.IO inside a loop of 500 tiny DB calls (switch cost plus pool pressure): batch instead.
  • CPU-heavy mapping of a large list on Main because "the repo is main-safe" was assumed, not implemented.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a Flow from Room need flowOn? -> No, Room runs the query on its own executor; apply flowOn for your own upstream CPU/IO work.
  2. Why inject dispatchers? -> Deterministic tests and a single place to swap pools.
  3. limitedParallelism use? -> Cap concurrency to one resource (e.g. a file writer) without a dedicated thread; verify against the coroutines version you ship.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use Dispatchers.IO in the repository." Senior: main-safety as contract, don't double-wrap main-safe libraries, inject dispatchers, CPU vs IO.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 12k-item sort ran on Main inside a "repository" function; p95 frame time spiked on low-end devices until it moved to Default.

questions.promptHtml: What is a single source of truth in the data layer, and what concrete breakage happens without one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most-asked data-layer question. Tests whether you can show the failure rather than recite a definition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For each piece of data, exactly one place holds the authoritative copy and everything the UI reads comes from it. Other sources feed it but are never shown directly. Without it, two screens hold two copies, a write updates one, and the user sees contradictory numbers. For offline-first apps the recommended SSOT is the local database.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The guide: the source of truth always contains consistent, correct, up-to-date data, and data the repository exposes should come directly from it. It can be the DB, an in-memory cache, or even the network (a payments repo may treat the server as truth; a login repo may treat its cache as truth). Per data type, not per app.

BROKEN                              CORRECT
Screen A <- API response copy       Screen A \
Screen B <- Room                    Screen B  >-- Room (SSOT) <-- repo writes from API
Write -> updates only Room          Write -> Room (+ queued sync)

Mechanism: network responses are written into the SSOT, the UI observes the SSOT, so a refresh is just "write to DB and the Flow re-emits". All consumers update together.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>> =
    dao.observeAll().map { rows -> rows.map(ArticleEntity::toModel) }   // only the DB is read

override suspend fun refresh() {
    dao.upsertAll(remote.latest().map(NetworkArticle::toEntity))        // network only writes
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning the network response to the caller and also writing to DB (two paths, they diverge on mapping bugs).
  • A StateFlow cache in the repository plus Room: two SSOTs; see Q129.
  • Treating "in-memory cache in the ViewModel" as the SSOT: it dies with the ViewModel.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can the network be the SSOT? -> Yes for always-online, server-authoritative data (balance); you accept no offline reads.
  2. What is the cost of DB-as-SSOT? -> Mapping, schema migrations, sync and conflict logic; not every screen deserves it.
  3. How does it interact with optimistic updates? -> Write locally first, mark pending, reconcile on sync (see Q127).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "database is the source of truth." Senior: it is per data type, shows the divergence bug, states the cost, and notes server-authoritative exceptions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Wishlist count differed between home and profile for 8% of users because one tab read a cached API list and another read Room.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app (2.1M DAU, 78% on Android 11-14, 22% on low-RAM devices) added a status field on the product API. A release goes out; the backend adds a new enum value "PREORDER" for 5% of products. Crash rate jumps from 0.3% to 2.4% on the product list. Stack excerpt:

kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException: ... does not contain element with name 'PREORDER'
  at ...ProductDto$$serializer.deserialize
  at com.shop.data.ProductRepository.getProducts(ProductRepository.kt:31)

Code:

@Serializable
data class ProductDto(val id: String, val name: String, val status: ProductStatus, val price: Double)
enum class ProductStatus { IN_STOCK, OUT_OF_STOCK }

class ProductRepository(private val api: ShopApi) {
    suspend fun getProducts(): List<ProductDto> = api.products()   // returned to ViewModel and Compose UI
}

Other teams already use ProductDto in the cart screen, the Room entity (annotated twice), and the analytics logger. Rollback of the backend is not possible for 6 hours.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through what is wrong architecturally, how you stop the crashes now, and how you prevent the class of bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add PREORDER to the enum and ship a hotfix." That fixes today's value and leaves the design: the next unknown value crashes again, and 2.1M users wait for a store rollout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the failure only list parsing or also cart/detail? (blast radius). Do we have a server-driven kill switch or remote config? Is the enum used in when expressions without else? Can the backend temporarily stop sending PREORDER to old clients (versioned header)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ask backend to filter or map PREORDER to IN_STOCK for app versions below the fix via the app-version header; halt the staged rollout if the bad build is the client; push a remote-config flag to hide the affected section if one exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) strict enum deserialization on an external contract; (b) DTO leaking into UI so one parse failure kills the whole list, not one item; (c) missing contract tests; (d) red herring: the crash started with the app release, but the trigger is the backend change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce in a unit test with the raw JSON; grep for ProductDto usages across modules; check Crashlytics for the 2.4% split by app version (all versions or only strict ones).
  5. Root cause: The repository returns the wire model, so the app's compile-time type is the server's contract. An unknown enum value throws during deserialization, which fails the entire response (one bad item kills 40).
  6. Fix: Short-term hotfix: Json { coerceInputValues = true; ignoreUnknownKeys = true } plus a default, val status: ProductStatus = ProductStatus.UNKNOWN, with @JsonNames/a fallback serializer (coerceInputValues works for enums only when the property has a default; verify with your serialization version). Long-term: separate ProductDto (internal to the data module) from Product (domain/UI), map in the repository, treat unknown as Unknown, and drop or degrade only the one item.
internal fun ProductDto.toDomain(): Product? = runCatching {
    Product(id, name, status.toDomain(), Money(price))
}.getOrNull()   // log + skip, never fail the whole list

// repository
suspend fun getProducts(): List<Product> = api.products().mapNotNull { it.toDomain() }
  1. Prevention: internal DTOs so other modules cannot import them; contract test feeding unknown enum/unknown field/null into the parser; when over domain sealed type with explicit Unknown; log unknown values to analytics to detect drift.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make every DTO field nullable (shifts crashes to NPE-style checks everywhere). I would not skip mapping "to save boilerplate"; that is the boilerplate that buys safety. Mapping cost is small: for 40 items it is microseconds.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Backend adds a required field you do not know about? -> ignoreUnknownKeys = true ignores it; only break if the type of an existing field changes.
  • What if the unknown status means "do not sell"? -> Unknown must map to the conservative behavior (hide Buy), decided by product, not by the default parser.
  • Should the domain enum be exhaustive? -> Yes plus Unknown; exhaustive when in UI forces a decision for each state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a payments app mapped DTOs in the repo but one screen imported the DTO "for speed". The one screen was the only one that crashed in the incident, and it became the proof that point for the architecture review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds the enum value and calls it done; no mention of DTO leakage.
  • Hire: lenient parsing plus a mapping layer; mentions mapNotNull and tests.
  • Strong hire: also contains blast radius, server-side mitigation, internal visibility, contract tests, unknown-value telemetry, and conservative semantics for unknown.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the caching strategies a repository can use (in-memory, disk, cache-aside, stale-while-revalidate, TTL). How do you choose, and where do you invalidate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you treat caching as a policy decision with invalidation cost, not a map you stick in a singleton.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I pick by how stale the data may be and how expensive a miss is. In-memory for session-lifetime lookups, disk (Room/DataStore) for data that must survive process death and offline use. Cache-aside means the repository checks the cache, falls back to the source, and fills the cache. Stale-while-revalidate shows cached data immediately and refreshes in the background, which gives the best perceived latency. The hard part is invalidation: a TTL, an explicit invalidate on write, or server-driven (push/ETag).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cache-aside      : read cache -> miss -> read source -> put cache -> return
Read-through     : same but the cache component hides the fallback
Write-through    : write cache + source together (consistent, slower writes)
Write-behind     : write cache, queue the source write (fast, needs durable queue)
SWR              : emit cached, launch refresh, emit fresh (Flow emits twice)

On Android the usual realization: Room as disk cache and SSOT, an in-memory layer only for hot, cheap-to-rebuild data (e.g. a config object). Network-layer HTTP caching (OkHttp Cache, ETag, Cache-Control) is a separate, complementary layer and is not a replacement for domain-level policy (A5 covers OkHttp detail).

Invalidation options: TTL (fetchedAt column, refresh if older than N minutes), event-based (invalidate on user action or push message), version/ETag (conditional GET returns 304, cheap). Choose per data type: feed 2 min, profile 1 day, country list 30 days.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun refreshIfStale(maxAge: Duration = 5.minutes) {
    val last = dao.lastFetchedAt() ?: 0L
    if (clock.millis() - last < maxAge.inWholeMilliseconds) return
    dao.upsertAll(remote.latest().map { it.toEntity(fetchedAt = clock.millis()) })
}

Inject a Clock/time source so TTL tests are deterministic.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• An unbounded mutableMapOf cache in a singleton: memory growth and no process-death survival.
  • A cache that is not keyed by user/locale/account; logout leaves the previous user's data (see Q129 and A4 session chunk).
  • Caching errors (empty list after a failed fetch) so the failure persists for the TTL.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not cache in the ViewModel? -> Dies with the screen scope, not shared between screens, lost on process death.
  2. How does a write invalidate reads? -> If reads observe the DB, the write updates it and the Flow re-emits; no manual invalidation.
  3. How to avoid 50 simultaneous refreshes? -> Deduplicate in-flight work with a shared deferred or Mutex (see Q131).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cache in a map or in Room." Senior: names the strategy, picks a TTL per data class, handles invalidation and failure caching, and keys caches by identity.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Currency conversion rates cached forever in memory; users who left the app open across a rate change checked out at a stale price until a refund spike showed it.

questions.promptHtml: Is a pass-through repository an anti-pattern? How do you decide whether a repository earns its existence?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates "pattern-matching" engineers from those who weigh cost. The official docs themselves show a pass-through, so a blanket "bad" answer is wrong.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A repository that forwards one call to one source with no mapping, caching or policy is not wrong, it is just not paying for itself yet. The official guide even starts with exactly that and says to split when a second source arrives. I keep it if it protects a boundary (mapping DTO to model, error translation, a seam for tests, a stable contract across modules). If it does none of that, I inject the DAO or service directly into the use case and delete the layer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cost of a repository: an interface, an implementation, a fake, DI binding, mapping code. Value: boundary stability, one place for policy, testability, module decoupling. Decide with a checklist:

Question If yes, the repository earns its keep
More than one source or an in-memory/disk cache? Policy lives here
Do wire/DB models differ from what the app needs? Mapping boundary
Is it consumed from more than one module/feature? Stable contract (api module)
Do errors need translation (HttpException to domain error)? Error boundary
Do tests need a fake for it? Seam

If every answer is no and the "repository" is 12 lines forwarding to Retrofit, keep the interface out of domain, or skip it. Worse than a pass-through: a repository with a method per screen (getHomeScreenData()), a "god" repository, or one that returns DTOs. Those add cost and take away the benefit.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Pass-through: no value yet
class TipsRepository(private val api: TipsApi) {
    suspend fun tips() = api.tips()
}
// Earning its keep: maps, translates errors, owns the cache
class TipsRepository(private val api: TipsApi, private val dao: TipDao) {
    fun observe(): Flow<List<Tip>> = dao.observe().map { it.map(TipEntity::toModel) }
    suspend fun refresh() = dao.replaceAll(api.tips().map { it.toEntity() })
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mechanical "every API gets a repository + use case + mapper" rule, which produces 3 classes of boilerplate per endpoint.
  • Deleting the layer on a startup of 3 engineers and then needing it back in 6 months; leave the seam cheap (interface + one impl in the same file).
  • Confusing a pass-through with a bad abstraction: the real harm is a leaky abstraction.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A team revolts against boilerplate; what do you propose? -> Per-feature criteria above, allow direct DAO/service use where the checklist is all "no", enforce no DTO leaks with an architecture test.
  2. Does a pass-through ever help? -> For modular apps: it is the only thing other modules see, so internals can change.
  3. How do you keep mapping cheap? -> Extension functions next to the models, no mapper class hierarchies.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "always use repository for clean architecture." Senior: judges by cost vs boundary value with a checklist and knows the official guide is not dogmatic.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team deleted 14 pass-through repos and saved ~600 lines; the one that fronted an auth-sensitive API they kept, and it later absorbed a token-refresh change without touching callers.

questions.promptHtml: How would you model errors from the data layer: exceptions, kotlin.Result, or a sealed result type? What do you pick for a large app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: There is no single answer; the signal is whether you weigh typed-ness, cancellation safety, Flow compatibility and ergonomics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The official guide accepts exceptions (try/catch in suspend, catch in Flow) and a Result wrapper. I use exceptions internally and expose a sealed domain result or typed domain exceptions at the repository boundary for errors the UI must handle differently, such as no network, unauthorized, validation. Unexpected bugs stay exceptions. Cancellation must always propagate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Approach Strength Weakness
Throw exceptions Idiomatic coroutines, no wrapping Callers can forget to catch; untyped; Flow ends on throw
kotlin.Result<T> Stdlib, forces handling Error type is Throwable (untyped); runCatching catches CancellationException; return-type use has had compiler restrictions historically (verify for your Kotlin version, 2.x relaxed many)
Sealed result (Success/Error(DomainError)) Exhaustive when, typed errors Boilerplate, every layer wraps/unwraps, still need to guard cancellation
Third-party (Arrow Either, kotlin-result) Typed errors, operators Dependency, team learning curve

Rules I follow: (1) errors the user can act on are values (modeled); programmer errors and truly exceptional cases are exceptions; (2) never catch CancellationException without rethrowing; (3) translate infra exceptions (HttpException, IOException, SQLiteException) to domain errors at the repository boundary; (4) in streams, model failure as a state in the stream if you want it to continue (see Q122).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface DataError {
    data object NoNetwork : DataError
    data object Unauthorized : DataError
    data class Server(val code: Int) : DataError
    data class Unknown(val cause: Throwable) : DataError
}
sealed interface Outcome<out T> {
    data class Ok<T>(val value: T) : Outcome<T>
    data class Fail(val error: DataError) : Outcome<Nothing>
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• try { } catch (e: Exception) in suspend code: catches CancellationException, breaks structured concurrency (see Q120).
  • Exposing Throwable to the UI; the UI maps strings from exception messages.
  • Modeling every conceivable error as a type: 25 subclasses nobody handles differently.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not Result<T> as return type? -> Untyped failure and runCatching cancellation trap; fine for small apps if wrapped carefully.
  2. Where does the user-facing message come from? -> The UI layer maps DataError to a string resource; the data layer never knows about strings.
  3. How do errors cross a KMP boundary to Swift? -> Exceptions need @Throws; sealed result types are friendlier (see Q133).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "try/catch and show a toast." Senior: classifies errors as expected vs bugs, types the expected ones, protects cancellation, and picks one convention per codebase.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app mapped every failure to "Something went wrong"; support tickets for expired sessions looked identical to outages.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (400k DAU) shows an order screen. QA reports: after tapping back quickly while loading, the next screen shows a stale-looking spinner for 2-3 seconds, and analytics shows order_load_failed events with message "Job was cancelled" at 11% of loads. Battery team notes extra radio wake-ups. The code:

class OrderRepository(private val api: OrderApi) {
    suspend fun load(id: String): Result<Order> = runCatching { api.get(id).toDomain() }
}

class OrderVm(private val repo: OrderRepository) : ViewModel() {
    fun load(id: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        repo.load(id)
            .onSuccess { _state.value = Content(it) }
            .onFailure { log("order_load_failed", it.message); _state.value = Error }
        prefetchRelated(id)       // second network call
    }
}

There is a red herring: someone suggests the OkHttp timeout is too low (it is 30s and unrelated).
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, what exactly happens at runtime, and how do you fix and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase timeouts" or "ignore the cancelled events in analytics". The first treats the wrong cause; the second leaves the extra work running.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the spurious failure correlate with navigation away? (cancellation signature). Is prefetchRelated also running after cancellation? (extra radio). What Kotlin/coroutines versions? (affects nothing, but I want to confirm no custom handler).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Filter CancellationException out of the analytics event now to stop the false alarm, and ship the real fix next release. Do not roll back; user impact is wasted work and bad metrics, not data loss.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) runCatching swallowing CancellationException; (b) screen-scope cancelled by back navigation; (c) timeouts (red herring: they would show SocketTimeoutException, not "Job was cancelled").
  4. How I'd verify: Unit test with StandardTestDispatcher, cancel the job mid-call and assert the coroutine stops; look at the analytics it::class.
  5. Root cause: When the ViewModel scope is cancelled, the suspended api.get throws CancellationException. runCatching catches Throwable, returns it as a failure value, and the coroutine keeps running as if nothing happened. It then logs failure, writes Error state, and runs prefetchRelated, which is a suspension point and will normally throw at the next cancellation check, but non-suspending parts and anything started with a different scope still run. Structured concurrency relies on the exception propagating.
  6. Fix: Rethrow cancellation.
suspend fun load(id: String): Result<Order> = try {
    Result.success(api.get(id).toDomain())
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
} catch (e: Exception) {
    Result.failure(e)
}
// or a shared helper:
inline fun <T> suspendRunCatching(block: () -> T): Result<T> =
    try { Result.success(block()) } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Throwable) { Result.failure(e) }

Long term: ban bare runCatching in suspend code with a detekt custom rule or an architecture test. 7. Prevention: Unit test per repository: cancel and assert no onFailure; lint/detekt rule; code review checklist. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch Throwable anywhere in suspend code (also swallows OOM). I would not replace the Result type just because of this; a helper fixes it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about withTimeout? -> TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException subtype; rethrowing it hides the timeout from a caller that wanted to handle it; use withTimeoutOrNull when you do.
  • Flow catch operator and cancellation? -> It does not catch the collector's cancellation, so Flow-based code avoids this trap.
  • Does viewModelScope cancellation also cancel async children? -> Yes, structured concurrency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team found a "failed to sync" metric that rose with every release, and every spike matched screens being closed faster after a UI speed-up. The metric was cancellations dressed as failures.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames timeouts or filters analytics only.
  • Hire: identifies runCatching swallowing cancellation and rethrows.
  • Strong hire: also reasons about continuing work after swallowed cancellation, adds a test and a lint rule, and discusses withTimeout subtleties.

questions.contextHtml:
A ride-hailing app (1.4M DAU, 35% on 3G/flaky networks in the target market) shows the same dialog for every failure: "Something went wrong. Try again." Support receives 9,000 tickets/week; 41% are "app says error but my internet is fine". After a backend deploy, 6% of users get HTTP 401 on /rides because their refresh token was rotated; they keep tapping Retry and get banned by the rate limiter (429). The data layer:

suspend fun rides(): List<Ride> = try { api.rides().map { it.toDomain() } } catch (e: Exception) { emptyList() }

Crash rate is fine (0.2%), p95 latency fine. Dashboards show no errors because everything is "handled".
questions.promptHtml: How do you redesign error handling across the repository boundary, and how do you handle the 401/429 loop right now?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Show the exception message in a toast." That leaks internals, is untranslated, and still does not distinguish retryable from non-retryable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 401 handled by an OkHttp authenticator already? Does 429 return Retry-After? Which screens consume rides() (does an empty list mean "no rides" or "failed")? Can the backend add an error code in the body?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop auto-retry on 401/429 (circuit-break in the UI: disable Retry with a countdown from Retry-After); server side raise the rate-limit for the affected cohort; hot-fix the 401 path to trigger re-login.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) swallowed errors turn failures into empty lists (data lie); (b) no error taxonomy: UI cannot choose action; (c) auth failures not routed to the session layer; (d) red herring: 3G latency (p95 fine).
  4. How I'd verify: Log the exception class distribution at the repository (HttpException code, IOException, SerializationException); replay with MockWebServer returning 401/429/500/timeout; check the Retry-After header.
  5. Root cause: catch (e: Exception) conflates "no data" with "failed to get data", and the UI has no information to pick an action. A 401 is not retryable until re-auth; a 429 requires waiting.
  6. Fix: Translate at the boundary:
internal fun Throwable.toDataError(): DataError = when (this) {
    is HttpException -> when (code()) {
        401 -> DataError.Unauthorized
        429 -> DataError.RateLimited(response()?.headers()?.get("Retry-After")?.toLongOrNull())
        in 500..599 -> DataError.Server(code())
        else -> DataError.Client(code())
    }
    is IOException -> DataError.NoNetwork       // includes timeouts
    is SerializationException -> DataError.Malformed
    else -> DataError.Unknown(this)
}

UI maps DataError to copy and actions: NoNetwork -> "Check connection" + Retry; Unauthorized -> route to login (via session layer); RateLimited -> disable Retry for N s; Server -> "We are having trouble" + Retry with backoff. Keep cached data visible with an error banner instead of an empty list. 7. Prevention: Report DataError types to analytics (so dashboards show real failures); repository tests with MockWebServer for each class; an architecture rule that no Exception catch returns an empty default. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a retry interceptor for 401/429. I would not model all 4xx as separate types; only the ones that change behavior.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should the repository retry automatically? -> Only idempotent reads on IOException, with capped exponential backoff and jitter; never for non-idempotent writes without an idempotency key.
  • Where does the 401 handling live? -> OkHttp authenticator for refresh; repository surfaces Unauthorized when refresh fails (auth detail is A7).
  • How to test the mapping? -> Table-driven unit test per exception/status.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team replaced 14 catch (e: Exception) blocks with one mapper and the support ticket category "app error" dropped into four actionable ones within a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blanket toast or retry.
  • Hire: typed errors, distinguishes retryable vs not, keeps cached data.
  • Strong hire: also handles Retry-After, idempotency, auth routing, analytics on error types, and cancellation safety.

questions.promptHtml: A repository exposes Flow<List<Item>>. Where do errors surface, what does the catch operator actually do, and how do you keep a UI stream alive after a failure?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates think catch makes the Flow resilient; it does not, and offline-first apps depend on this.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Flow that throws terminates. catch handles exceptions from upstream only, lets you emit a fallback value or rethrow, but the original stream is still over. To keep going you either retry/retryWhen (resubscribe), or you model the failure as a value in the stream (Loading/Content/Error) and resubscribe on user retry. Exceptions thrown downstream in collect are not caught by catch above.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The official offline-first guide notes the same: catch only prevents the crash; the backing Flow still terminates, and retry is the way to resume.

upstream (Room/network) -> map -> catch {..} -> stateIn -> collect
        throws here           ^ handled        ^ errors in collect: NOT handled by catch above

Patterns:

  • Local DB flow: errors are rare; catch { emit(Error) } is okay as a last-resort safeguard.
  • Network-driven flow (polling/sockets): retryWhen { cause, attempt -> if (cause is IOException && attempt < 3) { delay(1000L shl attempt.toInt()); true } else false }.
  • Better for UI: keep data flow and refresh failure separate. Data Flow comes from the DB (never fails because of the network); refresh errors come from suspend refresh() and surface via an event/state field, so a failed refresh does not kill the data stream.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val ui: StateFlow<ItemsUi> = repo.observeItems()
    .map<List<Item>, ItemsUi> { ItemsUi.Content(it) }
    .retryWhen { cause, attempt -> cause is IOException && attempt < 3 && true.also { delay(1_000L shl attempt.toInt()) } }
    .catch { emit(ItemsUi.Error) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ItemsUi.Loading)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Placing catch after stateIn/collect and thinking it covers upstream (it must be upstream of the collection).
  • Expecting catch to continue emitting from upstream; it cannot.
  • Swallowing CancellationException in a hand-written try inside flow {}.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does catch see exceptions thrown in collect? -> No; those belong to the collector (use try/catch there or onEach + catch).
  2. Why separate refresh errors from data? -> A network failure should not blank the cached list.
  3. What does retry do to side effects? -> Re-subscribes upstream, re-running side effects; keep upstream pure/idempotent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use catch in the ViewModel." Senior: knows catch only handles upstream and the flow terminates, picks retry vs error-as-state, and separates data flow from refresh errors.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed screen froze permanently after one transient SQLite exception because the catch emitted Error and the Flow was never re-collected until the process restarted.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (900k DAU) has a "Mark all as read" action and a feed refresh. Users report that when they tap Refresh then leave the screen within ~1 s (common on 4G with 1.8 s p50 latency), the feed is still stale next time and the server logs show half-completed sync calls. Telemetry: 14% of refreshes cancelled by navigation. Code:

class FeedRepository(private val api: FeedApi, private val dao: FeedDao) {
    suspend fun refresh() {
        val items = api.feed()                  // 1.8 s
        dao.clear()                             // step 2
        dao.insertAll(items.map { it.toEntity() })  // step 3
    }
}
class FeedVm(private val repo: FeedRepository) : ViewModel() {
    fun refresh() { viewModelScope.launch { repo.refresh() } }
}

Red herring: someone blames Room write-ahead logging.
questions.promptHtml: What can go wrong, and how should scope ownership and atomicity be designed?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in NonCancellable." That makes everything uncancellable, including the network call, and hides the design problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this a UI-oriented or app-oriented operation (should it complete if the user leaves)? Is the data needed offline? Does any other screen depend on it? How big is the payload?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the DB replace atomic so an interrupted refresh cannot leave an empty table (this is the user-visible damage if cancellation hits between clear() and insertAll).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cancellation between clear and insert leaves empty or partial data; (b) the refresh is tied to the screen's lifetime although the result is app-wide data; (c) no single-flight so double taps start two refreshes; (d) red herring: WAL (it does not cause lost refreshes).
  4. How I'd verify: Test with a fake API that suspends, cancel the scope between steps and assert table content; check the DB state after cancel.
  5. Root cause: refresh() runs in the caller's scope, so leaving the screen cancels it. Network call is fine to cancel, but the two DB steps are not atomic: cancellation points between them can leave the cache empty.
  6. Fix: (1) Atomic replace in one transaction (@Transaction suspend fun replaceAll(items)). (2) Decide ownership: if the data is app-oriented, the repository runs the work in an injected application-level scope and the caller awaits it:
class FeedRepository(
    private val api: FeedApi, private val dao: FeedDao,
    private val appScope: CoroutineScope,           // SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.Default, injected
) {
    suspend fun refresh() {
        appScope.async {
            val items = api.feed()
            dao.replaceAll(items.map { it.toEntity() })   // single transaction
        }.await()
    }
}

If the caller is cancelled, await throws but the async continues and the data lands. This matches the pattern described in the official data-layer guide for operations that must outlive the screen. 7. Prevention: Repository tests that cancel mid-flight; a rule that DB multi-step writes are in a transaction; single-flight for refresh (Q131). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use GlobalScope (no structure, no test control, no exception handling); I would not make everything app-scoped, because user-initiated, screen-bound work (search typing) should cancel with the screen. For must-survive-process-death work (upload) I use WorkManager, not app scope.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Exceptions in the app-scope coroutine? -> async stores them for await; with launch use a CoroutineExceptionHandler and SupervisorJob so one failure doesn't cancel siblings.
  • How do tests control appScope? -> Inject TestScope/backgroundScope.
  • What if the process is killed mid-refresh? -> Transaction rolls back; the next launch refreshes again (idempotent).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team saw "empty feed on cold start" for 0.7% of users; it was an interrupted clear-then-insert. One @Transaction removed the entire ticket class.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: NonCancellable or ignores atomicity.
  • Hire: transaction plus app-level scope with async/await.
  • Strong hire: also distinguishes UI/app/business-oriented operations, mentions WorkManager boundary, exception handling and test injection of scope.

questions.promptHtml: Should a repository own a CoroutineScope? How do you design lifecycle and thread ownership inside the data layer without leaking work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes structured-concurrency judgment at the architecture level: who owns background work, and who cancels it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Default to no: expose suspend and Flow and let the caller's scope own the work. A repository needs its own scope only for work that must outlive the caller: app-oriented operations (cache fill, sync), or hot shared state such as stateIn/shareIn. In that case the scope is injected (never created inline), with a SupervisorJob, a default dispatcher, and an owner that is responsible for cancelling it, and the repository's lifetime matches the scope's.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Official classification: UI-oriented (cancel when leaving screen), app-oriented (live while the app lives), business-oriented (must survive process death: WorkManager). The repository's scope is for the middle category.

caller scope (viewModelScope)  -> suspend call -> cancelled with the screen
appScope (Application, Supervisor) -> repo.async{} -> survives the screen, dies with process
WorkManager                   -> survives process death

Design rules: (1) inject the scope; a repository that builds CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) internally cannot be tested nor cancelled; (2) use SupervisorJob so one failed child doesn't cancel the others; (3) attach a CoroutineExceptionHandler for launch; (4) for user-scoped repositories (per-account) tie the scope to the session scope and cancel it on logout; otherwise work from account A writes into account B's store; (5) for hot state, stateIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) rather than a manual launch { collect { _state.value = it } }.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Singleton
class ConfigRepository @Inject constructor(
    remote: ConfigRemote,
    @ApplicationScope appScope: CoroutineScope,
) {
    val config: StateFlow<Config> = remote.stream()
        .stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), Config.Default)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• GlobalScope.launch inside repositories.
  • Repository creating CoroutineScope(Job()) per instance and never cancelling it, leaking per-user instances (see session/scoping chunk).
  • Using appScope.launch and returning immediately, so callers cannot observe failure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why SupervisorJob? -> A failing child otherwise cancels the scope and all siblings.
  2. Does WhileSubscribed need a scope? -> Yes, stateIn needs a scope for the sharing coroutine; it starts and stops upstream by subscribers.
  3. How to test? -> Provide backgroundScope from runTest so work ends with the test.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use Dispatchers.IO." Senior: classifies operations, injects scope, handles supervision and logout, and keeps caller-owned work caller-owned.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A per-account repo kept a private scope across account switch; late sync results from account A landed in B's UI for one second before a crash report exposed it.

questions.promptHtml: At the architecture level, what does offline-first require of the data layer, and when would you decide not to build it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you see offline-first as a cost/benefit decision with specific mechanics (read from local, writes strategy, sync), not a buzzword.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Minimum bar: the app can read without a network. That means a local source of truth that the UI observes, and the network only refreshes it. Writes are the hard part: online-only, queued, or lazy (local first then sync), each with different conflict risks. I only build it where the product demands it, such as flaky networks, field work, or content apps, because it adds sync, migrations and conflict logic.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the official guide: every repository that uses network has at least two sources (local and network); the local one is the SSOT; domain and UI never talk to network directly.

Write strategy Use when Risk
Online-only Bank transfer, checkout Must block UI offline
Queued writes Analytics, logs Loss acceptable
Lazy writes (local first, sync later) To-do notes, drafts Conflicts, needs versioning

Decision factors: connectivity profile of users (e.g. 35% on 3G), cost of staleness, whether server is authoritative, team capacity. Banking balance: server-authoritative, online-first with cached read-only view. Notes app: full offline writes. Do not default everything to a DB copy; the guide itself offers custom sync vs managed services (e.g. Firestore) as options (details of Room/WorkManager are A5).

Cost ledger: schema + migrations, mappers (network->entity->model), sync worker, retry/backoff, conflict policy, testing matrix (offline/online/flaky), larger APK/DB size.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class NotesRepository(private val dao: NoteDao, private val sync: SyncScheduler) {
    fun observe(): Flow<List<Note>> = dao.observeAll().map { it.map(NoteEntity::toModel) }
    suspend fun save(note: Note) {
        dao.upsert(note.toEntity(pending = true))   // local first
        sync.enqueue()                              // drained later with backoff
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming offline-first but still reading the network response directly in the UI.
  • No conflict story ("last write wins" chosen silently, losing edits).
  • Building full sync for content that changes hourly and is cheap to refetch.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Offline-first for a payments app? -> Reads yes (history), writes online-only.
  2. How do you show sync state? -> A syncState field per item (pending, failed) in the model.
  3. What does it do to testing? -> Adds offline/online/flaky permutations; fake network with a toggle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cache in Room and show it." Senior: separates reads and writes, picks write strategy per data type, names conflict policy and cost, and knows when not to.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team built bidirectional sync for a read-mostly catalog; 40% of its code was conflict handling that never triggered.

questions.contextHtml: A field-inspection app for utility technicians (12k users, 8 hours of shifts, 30-40% of time without connectivity, 150 forms/day/tech with photos up to 3 MB). Currently the app requires network for everything; techs write on paper and re-enter later. Product wants "works offline" in one quarter. Team: 4 Android engineers, backend team of 3 willing to add endpoints. Existing: Retrofit, Room (used for caching only), no sync code. Edits to the same form by two techs are rare (about 1 in 500) but happen.
questions.promptHtml: Design the data-layer approach: SSOT, write strategy, sync and conflicts, what you would cut from v1, and how you would ship it safely.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Room and WorkManager" with no write strategy, conflict policy, or photo handling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which data must be writable offline (forms only, or also assets)? Who wins on conflict, field data or office edits? Retention and device storage limits? Is data sensitive (encryption at rest)? Can backend provide per-record version or updatedAt and idempotent endpoints?
  2. Immediate mitigation (v0): Not an incident; I'd ship read-only offline first (download assigned jobs for the day) so value lands early and risk is low.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (design risks): (a) conflict and data loss on lazy writes; (b) photo uploads dominating sync time/battery; (c) schema migrations in the field; (d) partial sync leaving inconsistent relations.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype with a fault-injecting fake API (drop, duplicate, delay), instrumented offline/online toggling tests, dogfood 20 techs, measure sync success rate and bytes.
  5. Root cause (of the trade-off): Lazy writes are required (loss of a day's work is unacceptable), which forces local SSOT, versioning and idempotency.
  6. Fix (design): Room is SSOT; UI observes DAO Flows. Writes: local first with a syncState column (PENDING/SYNCED/FAILED) in the same transaction as the form. A SyncWorker (unique work, constraints CONNECTED, backoff) drains an outbox table in order; each operation carries a client-generated UUID as idempotency key so retries do not duplicate. Photos: separate upload queue (resumable, Wi-Fi preferred), form references photo IDs; form syncs when metadata is ready, photo can lag. Conflicts: per-record version; server rejects stale writes with 409; client for rare conflicts keeps both, flags for human resolution (last-write-wins is unsafe for inspection records). Pull: delta sync by updatedSince cursor, push notification triggers a sync (FCM data message to a worker). Encrypt DB (SQLCipher-class solution; verify licensing/choice).
@Entity data class OutboxOp(@PrimaryKey val opId: String, val formId: String, val type: String, val payload: String, val attempts: Int = 0)
  1. Prevention: Sync metrics (pending count, age of oldest pending, failure by type); a "sync now" and diagnostics screen; migration tests on seeded old DBs; cap on pending age alerts.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do CRDTs or field-level merge in v1 (cost vs 1-in-500 conflict). I would not offer offline editing of everything, just forms and notes. I would consider a managed sync service if the backend team cannot deliver versioned endpoints, accepting vendor lock-in.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tech reinstalls with unsynced data? -> Warn on logout/uninstall paths, block logout when outbox is not empty, show count.
  • Server clock skew? -> Use server-assigned versions, not device timestamps.
  • DB corruption? -> Export of pending outbox as a recovery path; integrity check on open.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped lazy writes with timestamp LWW, then discovered devices with wrong clocks silently overwrote newer edits. They moved to server versions plus 409.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Room plus WorkManager with no write or conflict design.
  • Hire: outbox, idempotency, versioned conflicts, phased delivery.
  • Strong hire: also separates photo queue, sync-state UX, metrics, clock-skew handling, and explicit cut list with managed-service alternative.

questions.promptHtml: Compare pull-based, push-based and hybrid synchronization, and explain how you would pick a conflict-resolution strategy.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Offline-first at senior level is about reconciliation. They want mechanics and trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Pull-based fetches on demand, usually before showing a screen: simple, but wasteful and weak for relational data. Push-based keeps a local replica and the server notifies you of changes: efficient and good offline, but needs versioning and server support. Most apps are hybrid: pull for high-churn feeds, push for user and settings data. For conflicts I choose by data value: last-write-wins for low-stakes data, versioned optimistic concurrency (reject stale writes) for important records, and field-level merge or CRDTs only when concurrent edits are common.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pull: Paging with RemoteMediator is the canonical Android form (navigation-driven fetch, persist, read from DB). Downsides: repeated visits refetch unchanged data, and relational models force cross-repository fetches. Push: initial baseline then deltas (updatedSince cursor, FCM "stale" signal, repo.sync()); the app tolerates long offline; needs versioning and awareness of local pending writes during sync.

Conflict strategies
LWW (timestamps)       cheap; loses edits; clock skew hazard (use server time)
Version / ETag (409)   safe; client must re-fetch and re-apply or ask the user
Field-level merge      fewer lost edits; more schema work
CRDT / OT              convergent; high complexity, usually a library or backend

Sync ordering: push local pending writes first, then pull deltas, so the pull does not overwrite unsynced local changes. Mark pending rows to make pull skip them (or merge by version).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun sync(): Boolean = try {
    pushPending()                                   // outbox first
    val delta = remote.changesSince(cursor.read())  // then pull
    dao.applyDelta(delta.items, skipPendingIds = dao.pendingIds())
    cursor.write(delta.cursor); true
} catch (e: IOException) { false }                  // false -> Result.retry() upstream

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using device wall-clock timestamps for LWW.
  • Pulling over unsynced local edits (user's change reverts on screen).
  • Treating a 409 as a generic failure and retrying forever.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which do you use for a social feed? -> Pull (Paging + RemoteMediator), with cachedIn.
  2. How do deletions sync? -> Tombstones or a deleted flag with version; otherwise pulls resurrect them.
  3. How do you handle a long offline gap? -> If cursor is older than server retention, do full resync.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "WorkManager syncs when online." Senior: pull/push/hybrid per data, ordering of push before pull, tombstones, versioning and clock-skew.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that pulled before pushing saw edits "snap back" for users returning online; reordering sync fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: Product asks for "infinite scroll of 2M listings with filters and offline support, and no duplicates or gaps". Current plan from a teammate: the ViewModel holds page: Int and appends api.list(page) results to a MutableStateFlow<List<Listing>>; filters reset the list. QA finds duplicates when new listings are posted between page fetches (feed shifts by 3-5 items/min), and after rotation scrolling restarts at the top; offline shows nothing. Page size 20, p50 latency 600 ms. Red herring: "make page size 100".
questions.promptHtml: Where should the pagination boundary sit between ViewModel, repository and network, and what would you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Paging 3" without explaining what it solves or where state lives.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is offline browsing of all pages needed or only the visited ones? Does the API offer cursor (keyset) pagination or only page numbers? How often does content change/ordering? Are filters server-side?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Dedupe by id when appending as a stopgap and persist the loaded list in the ViewModel/SavedState for rotation, to ship quickly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) offset/page-number pagination over a mutating list creates duplicates/gaps; (b) pagination state is in the ViewModel, so it is lost and not offline-capable; (c) no cache boundary; (d) page size is a red herring (bigger pages shift the same way).
  4. How I'd verify: Reproduce with a fake API inserting items between calls; check API for cursor support; test rotation with the state holder.
  5. Root cause: Offset pagination is not stable under inserts, and pagination state lives in the wrong layer.
  6. Fix: Ask backend for keyset/cursor pagination (stable under inserts). The repository owns loading, exposes Flow<PagingData<Listing>> (Paging 3: Pager + RemoteMediator writing pages and remote keys into Room, DB as SSOT), keyed by the filter; ViewModel applies cachedIn(viewModelScope) and passes only the filter as state; flatMapLatest on filter changes. Map entities to domain models with PagingData.map in the repository or ViewModel, not in the UI.
val listings: Flow<PagingData<Listing>> = filter.flatMapLatest { f ->
    repo.pager(f).flow.map { page -> page.map(ListingEntity::toModel) }
}.cachedIn(viewModelScope)

(Paging detail and Compose collectAsLazyPagingItems are A3/A5; I would also check Paging version for current API.) 7. Prevention: Tests for filter switch, refresh, process death; a monitored duplicate-id counter; contract that listing ids are unique and sorted. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hold 2M-item lists in memory or hand-roll gap/dup logic if Paging is available. If the team cannot adopt Paging, a hand-rolled version still belongs in the repository, not the ViewModel. If offline is only for visited pages, skip the RemoteMediator and use PagingSource with cachedIn first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Filters change while loading? -> flatMapLatest cancels the old pager.
  • Where do remote keys live? -> A table in the same DB, cleared with the data in one transaction.
  • Should domain layer know about PagingData? -> Debatable; it is a UI-adjacent type, many teams expose it from the repository anyway; state the choice.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a marketplace went from offset to cursor pagination and the "duplicate listing" support category disappeared overnight, with no client change besides keys.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: page counter in the ViewModel and bigger pages.
  • Hire: Paging 3 with RemoteMediator, DB as SSOT, filter via flatMapLatest.
  • Strong hire: also fixes root cause (cursor pagination with backend), discusses where PagingData sits, remote keys atomicity, and fallback options.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app (3M DAU). Since last release, 3% of users report "I changed my delivery address, the order screen still shows the old one" and, worse, after logout/login as a different account on shared tablets (restaurant staff), 0.4% see the previous account's saved addresses for a few seconds. Code (simplified):

@Singleton
class AddressRepository @Inject constructor(private val api: AddressApi, private val dao: AddressDao) {
    private val cache = MutableStateFlow<List<Address>>(emptyList())

    fun observe(): Flow<List<Address>> = merge(cache, dao.observe().map { it.map(AddressEntity::toModel) })

    suspend fun refresh() { cache.value = api.addresses().map { it.toModel() }; dao.replaceAll(cache.value.map { it.toEntity() }) }
    suspend fun update(a: Address) { api.update(a); dao.upsert(a.toEntity()) }   // cache not touched
}

Crash rate is normal (0.25%). Profile shows no ANRs. Red herring: someone suspects Room invalidation lag.
questions.promptHtml: Find the root cause(s), fix them under a release schedule of one hotfix per week, and prevent recurrence.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear the cache on update." That patches one symptom and ignores the double source of truth and the account leak.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does logout clear the DB and the singleton? Is the DB per account or shared? Does observe() order matter (merge interleaving)? Are there other repositories with the same pattern?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server flag or hotfix that makes observe() read only the DB; on logout clear DB and reset the singleton state. Sending users a forced sign-out is not needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) two sources of truth: cache and Room, merged so the latest emission from either wins, while update changes only Room, then merge shows whichever emitted last; (b) singleton state outlives the account; (c) refresh() writes cache before DB commit; (d) red herring: Room invalidation latency (typically ms).
  4. How I'd verify: Unit test: refresh, update, observe, assert latest; test logout then login as B and assert no A data; log emission source per update in a debug build.
  5. Root cause: merge of a memory flow and a DB flow has no defined winner. After update, the DB emits new data, but the StateFlow keeps the old list; on any later cache emission or a new collector, the stale list reappears. The singleton also holds account A's list when B logs in until a refresh replaces it.
  6. Fix: One source: Room only. observe() = DAO flow mapped to model. refresh() and update() write to Room (after the API succeeds), and the in-memory cache is deleted. Scope user data to the session: key the table by accountId and/or clear on logout in one transaction, or provide the repository from a user-scoped DI component that is destroyed on logout.
fun observe(accountId: String) = dao.observe(accountId).map { it.map(AddressEntity::toModel) }
suspend fun update(a: Address) { api.update(a.toDto()); dao.upsert(a.toEntity()) }
  1. Prevention: A rule of thumb in review: "one data type, one writer-visible store"; logout test in CI that asserts every user-scoped store empties; architecture test forbidding MutableStateFlow caches next to a DAO in repositories.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add manual cache invalidation calls everywhere (they are forgotten). In-memory speed is rarely needed because Room Flow emits within ms; if it is, derive the memory layer from the DB, not beside it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the API returns the updated entity? -> Write the server's version into Room, not the client's input.
  • Optimistic UI? -> Write local with pending, rollback on failure.
  • Shared tablets? -> Treat logout as a data boundary; encrypt and wipe per account.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a privacy review found a stale-singleton leak that took 10 minutes to fix, 3 days to audit, and led to a "user-scoped" DI component for all account data.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: invalidates the cache after update only.
  • Hire: removes the second source and fixes logout cleanup.
  • Strong hire: also reasons about merge semantics, user-scoped DI/tables, CI logout test and privacy impact.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test a repository? Fakes or mocks, and what do you actually assert?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether architecture decisions (interfaces, injected dispatchers) translate into trustworthy tests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I test repositories against fake data sources (in-memory implementations of the interfaces) and assert on behavior: what the Flow emits after a refresh, what is written locally, how errors map. I use real Room in-memory for DAO integration and MockWebServer for the HTTP boundary. I avoid verifying call counts on mocks, which test implementation, not behavior.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Test pyramid for the data layer:

  • Unit: repository + fake remote + fake local (fast, deterministic, covers policy: TTL, merge, error mapping).
  • Integration: real Room (in-memory) + real mapper + fake remote; real Retrofit with MockWebServer for serialization and status-code mapping.
  • Contract: the same test suite runs against the fake and the real implementation to keep the fake honest (important when fakes are used everywhere).

Fakes vs mocks: a fake has behavior (a list backing observable state); a mock records interactions. Fakes survive refactors; mocks break when you change how the repository calls its collaborators.

class FakeNewsRemote : NewsRemoteDataSource {
    var result: Result<List<NetworkArticle>> = Result.success(emptyList())
    override suspend fun latest() = result.getOrThrow()
}

@Test fun refresh_writes_remote_into_local() = runTest {
    val local = FakeNewsDao(); val remote = FakeNewsRemote().apply { result = Result.success(listOf(a1)) }
    val repo = NewsRepositoryImpl(remote, local)
    repo.refresh()
    assertEquals(listOf(a1.toModel()), repo.observeArticles().first())
}

Also test: cancellation, error mapping table, TTL with an injected clock, idempotent refresh, and Flow re-emission (Turbine).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dispatchers.IO hardcoded, making runTest non-deterministic.
  • Fake that is more permissive than the real thing (no unique constraint), so bugs pass.
  • Asserting verify(exactly = 1) { api.latest() } instead of the visible outcome.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is a mock acceptable? -> For verifying an outbound side effect with no observable state (e.g. analytics call).
  2. How do you test Room Flow invalidation? -> Real in-memory Room, insert and collect with Turbine.
  3. How do you keep fakes in sync with reality? -> Shared contract tests run against both.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "mock the API with Mockito." Senior: fakes plus contract tests, behavior assertions, injected dispatchers/clock, and an integration layer with real Room and MockWebServer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mock-heavy suite stayed green while the real DAO's unique index rejected a duplicate insert that the mocks happily accepted.

questions.contextHtml:
A trading-news app prepares for a marketing push: DAU 200k to 2M, with a push notification that opens the same "Top Story" screen for 1.2M users within 90 seconds. Backend rate limiter: 50k req/min per endpoint. In staging load-tests with the real client, /top-story receives 3-4 identical calls per app open (ViewModel refresh, a widget refresh, a prefetch worker, and a pull-to-refresh debounce failure), pushing the endpoint to 4x expected load. Code:

suspend fun topStory(): Story = api.topStory().toDomain()      // called by 4 sites, no coordination

p95 latency 700 ms normal; the backend team says anything above 50k/min returns 429.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change in the data layer so the client does not amplify load, without making the UI stale?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a delay/debounce in the ViewModel" (only one of four sources).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What freshness does product need (5 s? 60 s)? Is the story identical for all users (CDN-cacheable)? Can the backend send ETag/Cache-Control? Are all four call sites inside one process?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side CDN/caching for the endpoint; client hotfix is a short TTL (e.g. 30 s) in the repository so repeated callers read the cache.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no request coalescing (single-flight), (b) no TTL/ETag, (c) retry storms after 429 (no jitter), (d) red herring: p95 latency (not the issue; the count is).
  4. How I'd verify: Load test with request counters per call site; OkHttp event listener counts; MockWebServer to count calls in a unit test with 4 concurrent callers.
  5. Root cause: Each call site triggers its own network call; in the push burst they all fire at the same moment, multiplying load, and a 429 triggers synchronized retries.
  6. Fix: Single-flight plus TTL plus backoff with jitter, all in the repository:
class StoryRepository(private val api: StoryApi, private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val clock: Clock) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    private var inFlight: Deferred<Story>? = null
    private var cached: Pair<Long, Story>? = null

    suspend fun topStory(maxAgeMs: Long = 30_000): Story {
        cached?.takeIf { clock.millis() - it.first < maxAgeMs }?.let { return it.second }
        val d = mutex.withLock {
            inFlight?.takeIf { it.isActive } ?: scope.async {
                api.topStory().toDomain().also { cached = clock.millis() to it }
            }.also { inFlight = it }
        }
        return d.await()
    }
}

Four concurrent callers share one Deferred; callers that cancel do not cancel the shared call because it runs in the injected scope. Add HTTP caching headers (ETag/304 revalidation) and exponential backoff with jitter on 429 honoring Retry-After. Consolidate refresh triggers: widget and worker call the same repository method. Server: CDN, and per-client rate budget. 7. Prevention: Load test in CI for key endpoints with a request counter; client-side metric "requests per session per endpoint"; a code-review rule that network calls go through repositories only. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise the server rate limit as the only fix (hides amplification). Single-flight adds shared state and a subtle failure mode: if the shared call fails, all callers fail together; that is acceptable and desired. Per-process only: multiple processes (widget in another process) are not coordinated.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Stale-but-ok policy? -> Return cache and revalidate in the background (SWR), emitting twice via Flow.
  • What about per-user data? -> Key in-flight and cache by user/params.
  • Exception caching? -> Do not cache failures, but add a short negative cache/backoff to avoid a storm.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a launch-day load test showed 3.1 calls per open; after consolidating triggers and single-flight the number was 1.05, and the backend left its limits unchanged.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: debounce in the ViewModel only.
  • Hire: single-flight plus TTL in the repository.
  • Strong hire: also jitter/Retry-After, ETag, scope ownership of the shared call, keyed in-flight maps, and load-test metric.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide repository boundaries: per entity, per feature, or per aggregate? What goes wrong when repositories depend on each other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real codebases rot here: god repositories, cycles, and cross-repository transaction problems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One repository per data type or aggregate that has its own consistency rules, not per screen and not per table. A ProductRepository and an OrderRepository are different aggregates. Repositories may depend on others for aggregation, but only in one direction; cross-repository orchestration belongs in a use case or a coordinating repository, and anything needing atomicity across stores needs a transaction boundary at a single owner.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The data-layer guide allows multi-level repositories (UserRepository over LoginRepository and RegistrationRepository; some teams call these managers). Boundary smells:

Smell Symptom Fix
God repository 40 methods, 10 dependencies Split by aggregate/consistency boundary
Per-screen repo Same data fetched twice with different caches One repo per data type
Cycles A needs B, B needs A (DI cycle error) Extract shared part C; or use case on top
Cross-repo write Updates two stores, one fails One owner does the transaction; or outbox + eventual consistency
Repo calling ViewModel-ish logic Presentation formatting in data layer Move to UI/domain

For modular apps: the repository interface lives in an api/domain module, the implementation in data, so features depend only on contracts (see modularization chunk). A cycle between two repositories is a design bug, not a DI problem: fix the dependency direction, do not use Lazy/Provider to hide it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Use case coordinates; repositories stay independent
class PlaceOrder(private val cart: CartRepository, private val orders: OrderRepository) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(): OrderId {
        val items = cart.snapshot()
        return orders.place(items).also { cart.clear() }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Repository per DAO table, forcing joins in the UI layer.
  • Repository A injecting B's DAO "just this once", bypassing B's policy.
  • Lazy<B> injected to silence a Dagger cycle.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
