1. Cross-store atomicity? -> One transaction in a single database; across network+DB use an outbox and idempotent sync.
  2. Where does aggregation live: repo or use case? -> Data-shaped joins in the repo; business flows in use cases (domain is optional per the guide).
  3. How to enforce direction? -> Module boundaries or architecture tests on package dependencies.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "one repository per feature." Senior: per aggregate/consistency boundary, recognizes smells, resolves cycles by design, handles cross-store consistency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: UserRepository and SettingsRepository mutually depended; the team used Lazy and a race on startup produced a null token on first launch for 0.5% of installs.

questions.promptHtml: How would you structure the data layer for a Kotlin Multiplatform app shared with iOS? What do you share, what stays platform-specific, and what are the gotchas?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: KMP data-layer sharing is the most common first step; they want practical boundaries, not enthusiasm.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I share repositories, domain models, mappers, sync logic and networking in commonMain, with interfaces for platform things (secure storage, connectivity, file paths) implemented via expect/actual or injected. For libraries I use KMP-compatible ones: Ktor, kotlinx.serialization, kotlinx.coroutines, and a KMP database (SQLDelight, or Room KMP). Gotchas: Flow and exceptions across the Swift boundary, threading/dispatchers, iOS file paths for the DB, and library support differences.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
commonMain : Repository (interface + impl), models, mappers, DataError, sync logic
             Ktor client, kotlinx.serialization, DB access (SQLDelight / Room KMP)
androidMain: Android Context-dependent pieces (DB builder, connectivity, secure storage)
iosMain    : NSFileManager DB path, Keychain, Reachability, Ktor Darwin engine

Facts to verify before quoting versions: the Android docs describe Room as supporting KMP with a SQLiteDriver (the bundled driver is recommended), requires suspend DAO functions on non-Android targets, defaults its query context to Dispatchers.IO unless set, and leaves some Android-only features unavailable on other platforms (pre-packaged DB, multi-instance invalidation, auto-close). The currently fetched Room KMP page shows a room3 artifact on an alpha version; check the stable status of your target version (verify).

Boundary issues: (1) Swift sees Flow as an opaque Kotlin type; wrap with a platform-friendly adapter (callbacks/AsyncSequence bridges or a library) or expose snapshots. (2) Exceptions need @Throws to be visible to Swift; sealed result types cross the boundary more cleanly. (3) Coroutine scopes on iOS: provide a scope owned by the iOS app lifecycle, and mind Dispatchers.Main. (4) Keep DI simple (constructor injection or Koin; Hilt is Android-only).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// commonMain
interface TokenStore { suspend fun read(): String?; suspend fun write(t: String) }  // expect/actual or injected

class NewsRepositoryImpl(
    private val http: HttpClient,
    private val db: NewsDatabase,
) : NewsRepository {
    override fun observe(): Flow<List<Article>> = db.newsQueries.all().asFlow().mapToList(Dispatchers.Default).map { it.map(Row::toModel) }
}

(Uses SQLDelight's coroutine extensions; verify package names against your version.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sharing Android types (Context, Uri) in common models.
  • Using Result/exceptions that Swift cannot see.
  • Assuming JVM-only libraries (Retrofit, Gson) work in common.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why DB and network in the shared module and not UI? -> Highest reuse and lowest platform-API friction; UI sharing is a separate decision.
  2. Repository interface per platform? -> No: common interface, platform bits injected underneath.
  3. Testing? -> Common tests with fakes run on all targets (kotlin.test, runTest).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "put everything in shared." Senior: shares policy and data, keeps platform capabilities behind interfaces, knows the Swift interop costs, and flags library/status risks to verify.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared repository exposed Flow directly to Swift; iOS devs wrote brittle wrappers in three screens until a single bridge layer was added.

questions.contextHtml: A messaging app (6M DAU) stores drafts, notification prefs and last-read pointers in SharedPreferences (JSON blobs, up to 200 KB for 7% of users). Telemetry: SharedPreferences apply() ANR contributions on QueuedWork.waitToFinish account for 18% of ANRs (ANR rate 0.52%, above the 0.47% bad-behavior threshold I would verify in Play Console vitals). The plan is to migrate to DataStore (Proto) in 4 weeks, with weekly releases at staged rollout, and no loss of drafts. Existing code: 31 call sites read prefs directly from ViewModels and Activities.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate storage under live traffic without data loss, and how do you structure the code so the migration is safe and reversible?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace all call sites with DataStore in one PR." High blast radius, no rollback, no data-migration plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which keys are read synchronously at startup (blocking)? Multi-process access (widgets, services)? Is the data recoverable from the server if lost? What is the rollback window?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cheapest ANR reduction first: move commit()/apply() of large blobs off the main thread path where possible, and stop writing the 200 KB blob on every keystroke (debounce drafts). That buys time without migrating anything.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) large synchronous prefs writes flushing at lifecycle events (QueuedWork.waitToFinish); (b) scattered direct access makes any fix hard; (c) multi-process prefs; (d) red herring: Room (not involved).
  4. How I'd verify: Play Console ANR clusters with stack traces, StrictMode disk-write detection in debug builds, tracing of write sizes and frequency.
  5. Root cause: Large SharedPreferences writes flushed on the main thread at Activity stop; architecture-wise, storage is a direct dependency of 31 call sites, so changing the backing store is a 31-site change.
  6. Fix (phased): Phase 1: introduce UserPrefsDataSource interface and a repository UserPrefsRepository (Flow reads, suspend writes); first implementation wraps SharedPreferences. Migrate the 31 call sites behind it (no behavior change, safe to ship). Phase 2: add a DataStore implementation with a SharedPreferencesMigration that imports old values on first access (DataStore's migration mechanism; verify exact API for your version). Phase 3: remote-flag-controlled rollout (1% to 100%) selecting the implementation, with reads from the new store and the old store left intact until stable. Phase 4: after two stable releases, delete the old implementation and the legacy file.
interface UserPrefsDataSource {
    val prefs: Flow<UserPrefs>
    suspend fun update(transform: (UserPrefs) -> UserPrefs)
}
// DataStore impl: dataStore.updateData(transform) ; migrations = listOf(SharedPreferencesMigration(...))
  1. Prevention: Metric on ANR by stack; StrictMode in CI/debug; architecture test forbidding getSharedPreferences outside the data source; round-trip tests on pre-migration data fixtures (including the 200 KB case and corrupted JSON).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not dual-write forever (two stores, two truths); a bounded dual-read during the migration is enough. I would not flip everyone at once; a data bug in migration is unrecoverable for local-only data. Startup reads that must be synchronous may need a one-time blocking read or a small separate store; I'd measure before deciding.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rollback after migration ran? -> The old file is still there until phase 4; the flag reverts reads, but writes made in the new store would be lost: so keep the old file read-only and accept only recent-edit loss, or dual-write for one release.
  • Multi-process access? -> DataStore does not support multiple processes for the same file with the default API (verify against current docs); use the multi-process variant where available, or route through one process.
  • Where does the repository sit? -> It holds the policy (defaults, validation); the data source only does storage.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the interface-first phase alone removed 4 of the 5 ANR stacks, because it exposed and fixed three write-per-keystroke bugs. The storage swap was almost anticlimactic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang replacement.
  • Hire: interface behind a repository, phased rollout, built-in migration.
  • Strong hire: also mitigates ANRs first, defines rollback and data-loss analysis, uses flags, tests with real fixtures and prevents regressions with an architecture test.
